procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 29.01.2024 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in CRM-M No.24743 of 2023 cancelling the bail granted to the petitioner vide its Order dated 05.07.2021.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court initially granted bail to the petitioner on 05.07.2021 in CRM-M No.23889 of 2021 and on 21.09.2021 in CRM-M No.27365 of 2021. Subsequently, the NIA applied for cancellation of bail, and the High Court cancelled the bail by the impugned order dated 29.01.2024 in CRM-M No.24743 of 2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner, being aggrieved by the High Court's order cancelling bail, filed a Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 2819 of 2024 in the Supreme Court. The petitioner also filed a Writ Petition (Crl.) No.168 of 2024 raising similar questions of law and facts. The Supreme Court heard both petitions together and dismissed them.

decision.appeal_result: Special leave petition and writ petition dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned order cancelling the petitioner’s bail should be set aside and the earlier order granting bail be revived.

facts: The petitioner was granted bail by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana on 05.07.2021.
Subsequently, the National Investigation Agency (NIA) took over the investigation of the case.
At the NIA's request, the High Court cancelled the petitioner's bail in an order dated 29.01.2024.
The petitioner challenged this cancellation order in the Supreme Court.
The trial of the offences was transferred from a Special Court in Punjab to a Special Court in Gujarat to be tried along with other Scheduled Offences.
law: The NIA has the jurisdiction to investigate Scheduled Offences under the NIA Act, as well as any connected non-scheduled offences.
Under Section 14 of the NIA Act, connected offences can be tried together with Scheduled Offences.
application: The Court first determined that the NIA was justified in taking over the investigation of the offences alleged against the petitioner.

Because the NIA had proper jurisdiction and the trial was transferred to a Special Court in Gujarat to be tried with Scheduled Offences (under the UAPA), the Court found that the NIA was also justified in seeking the cancellation of the petitioner's bail.
The Court concluded that the High Court's decision to cancel the bail was correct in light of the transfer of the investigation and trial to the NIA and the Special Court in Gujarat.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's request to set aside the cancellation of his bail. It found that the NIA had proper jurisdiction over the case and was therefore justified in seeking the cancellation, especially since the trial had been transferred to be heard alongside related Scheduled Offences. Consequently, the Special Leave Petition was dismissed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the impugned order cancelling the petitioner’s bail should be set aside and the earlier order granting bail be revived.
appellant_arguments: The impugned order cancelling the petitioner’s bail should be set aside.
The earlier order dated 05.07.2021 granting bail should be revived.
respondent_arguments: The writ petition should be dismissed.
Section 6 and other provisions of the Act should be interpreted broadly to advance their object, not in the curtailed and narrow fashion submitted by the petitioner.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The expression 'the accused' in Section 8 of the NIA Act is not restricted to only the accused for whom the investigation was handed over by the Central Government. The NIA is empowered to investigate any other accused in respect of a Scheduled Offence that is connected with the original Scheduled Offence under investigation, and therefore, the scope of the NIA's powers under Section 8 must be interpreted expansively.
obiter: An interpretation that would advance the object of Section 6 and other provisions of the Act cannot be read in a curtailed and narrow fashion.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) Act must be interpreted broadly to advance its object of enabling national-level investigation and prosecution. Allowing the NIA to investigate accused persons under different FIRs registered in different states as connected offenses provides an enlarged scope for investigation into Scheduled Offences and fulfills the salutary statutory intent of Section 6(6) of the Act, which is to cull any duplicity of investigation.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a purposive interpretation of the statute, holding that Section 6 and other provisions of the Act must be read in a way that would advance their object and cannot be read in a curtailed and narrow fashion.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner's submission that the NIA should add accused from other FIRs to its investigation rather than treating other offenses as connected was rejected because the court found that such a course would lose sight of the salutary statutory intent to investigate and prosecute at a national level and, in particular, Section 6(6) of the Act which clearly envisions culling of any duplicity of investigation.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument for a broad interpretation of the NIA Act was accepted, as the court found that allowing the NIA to investigate accused persons under different FIRs registered in different States provides an enlarged scope to the investigation into the Scheduled Offences.

The court affirmed the NIA's broad authority by reasoning that Section 8 of the NIA Act applies not only when the Central Government directs an investigation under Section 6(5) but also when it acts on a report from a State Government under Section 6(4).
policy_considerations: Deep-rooted in our constitutional philosophy and social fabric is the vision to facilitate every citizen to be a constructive citizen, the best they can be. This vision hopes that the State’s obligation is met with a commitment to contribute as constructive citizens to the nation’s development.
Inextricably linked to this commitment is also the negative aspect of constructive citizenship, that is, to actively refrain from contributing against the interest of the community and the nation.
